    text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')

Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout') for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1)))

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer vision problem: editing an image toward a target emotion while preserving its scene. Requiring only an image and an emotion label offers an appealing interface for creative applications.

EmoPair provides a potentially valuable resource comprising 331,595 relabeled InstructPix2Pix pairs and 6,949 additional generated pairs. The manuscript attributes the principal source datasets and pretrained methods.

The qualitative examples demonstrate plausible changes beyond recoloring, including object replacement and expression editing. The randomized human preference study provides independent evidence of some benefit, with approximately 56% overall preference over the selected baselines.

The supplementary material includes ablations, evaluation interfaces, and failure examples. The discussion appropriately acknowledges semantic drift, facial artifacts, and potential misuse for emotional manipulation.
weaknesses: The automatic evaluation is strongly coupled to the method. The same predictor P labels or filters training data, selects outputs over up to 30 inference iterations, and supplies EMR, ESR, and ENRD. Table 1 shows EMR falling from 50.20% to 5.06% without P. Baselines are not given comparable selection procedures or generation budgets, so the results do not isolate improved editing from optimization against the evaluator. Independent evaluation and matched-selection controls are needed.

The training objective is unclear in a consequential way. Section 3.2 defines z = E(Is), noises this source latent, and trains noise prediction without introducing the paired target image into the objective. Read literally, this trains source reconstruction rather than supervised editing. This may be a notation error, but it must be resolved. Section S2.2 also omits learning rate, batch size, training duration, and essential sampling settings; a promised release does not resolve these reproduction gaps.

The claimed architectural and reasoning novelty is insufficiently established. Since the emotion encoder receives only an eight-way label, its output is identical across images with the same target emotion. Its alignment loss therefore cannot itself represent source-specific editing instructions. Claims of human-like neuro-symbolic reasoning exceed the evidence, and comparisons against simpler learned category embeddings or conventional emotion-conditioned InstructPix2Pix are missing.

Several baselines are weakly configured: InstructPix2Pix and CLIP-Styler receive single-word prompts despite the manuscript explicitly identifying their ineffectiveness. LMS is a useful stronger comparison, but the cited Affective Image Filter is not evaluated. These choices weaken claims of superiority over existing emotional editing approaches.

The metrics need stronger justification. ESR uses KL divergence from a predicted distribution to an exact one-hot vector; under the standard definition this is infinite when non-target probabilities are positive. The implemented direction or smoothing must be specified. Furthermore, low Grad-CAM activation does not establish emotional neutrality, and edge similarity does not establish semantic preservation. The human study evaluates emotional preference without directly testing preservation of the source scene.

The human evidence supports a narrower conclusion than the broad superiority claims. Figure S7 reports 54% preference over LMS online and 49% in the small lab study, while negative-emotion transfers favor NST and CLIP-Styler. Trial reporting also needs reconciliation: 417 participants completing 100 trials gives 41,700 trials, not 417,000, and the supplement reports 11,400 after filtering. The sampling unit for standard errors and treatment of repeated participant/image judgments are unspecified. Within-valence and neutral-image generalization are supported only qualitatively.

The dataset contribution lacks independent quality validation. Most pairs receive automatic emotion labels from a predictor with 73% reported EmoSet accuracy, without a human audit of the resulting labels or preservation quality. Figure S3 includes substantial semantic replacements, such as food becoming a landscape. Transition distributions and subset ablations are absent, leaving the reliability and distinct benefit of the curated data uncertain.
